A notable and underappreciated driver is that 33% of AMP's profit now comes from managing Chinese pension assets, where AMP still has a strong brand. With 2.6 trillion dollars in the Chinese pension system, there is meaningful growth potential. The company announced a $150 million on-market buyback and the dividend came in higher than expected. At 15 times earnings Clark holds but won't commit to a buy.

headline: Ben Clark rates Mineral Resources a buy after strongest result in 20 years with debt dramatically reduced and FY27 guidance impressive
reasoning: Mineral Resources delivered what Clark considers the highlight of TMS Private's portfolio through reporting season, with all mining assets delivering higher output guidance and lower cost guidance simultaneously. The debt-to-EBITDA ratio has fallen to 1.2 times post the Posco sale, an extraordinary turnaround from the balance sheet fears of 12-24 months ago. Clark credits new chairman Malcolm Blundell with disciplining CEO Chris Ellison and restoring strategic focus. He believes the lithium supply shortage persists at least until 2030 and sees the stock reaching $100 in coming years. The company is also exploring copper acquisitions as the next growth leg.
quote: I put it was probably the the highlight of the stocks that we own through the reporting season in terms of how strong the numbers were versus expectations and what I was really happy about was also the guidance for FY27 it's all of their mining assets came in with higher output guidance and lower cost guidance so that the company is really hitting its straps now initially the market loved the result and I think it nearly hit $75 and then we had the earnings call and and Chris sort of dropped the semi-bomb sort of saying we're looking at offshore looking at buying something offshore looking at copper we're looking at the next leg of growth so which I think you know is interesting but you know a year or half two years ago the mark was freaked out about this company's balance sheet and you know it's just incredible how quickly that has swung around the debt to EBITDA is now trading at 1.2 times post the Posco sale that they'll be doing fairly soon and you know it feels like this is a really high quality business in the mining space and it's back hitting the ball out of the ballpark and I think there's a lot more ahead of it so you know I can see this stock you know going to $100 over the next few years because I think this lithium story like I listened to Pilbara's result as well not the way I'm Pilbara but the CEOs print seem pretty adamant that there's a supply shortage at least till 2030 in that space.

headline: Ben Clark sells Sims as cyclical peak play with brutal downside risk when steel and scrap cycle turns
reasoning: The US steel price has been very strong this year and scrap prices follow on from steel, driving Sims' earnings rebound. The company is good at managing what it can control and the US expansion has been positive. However, it is a highly cyclical business with high fixed costs, meaning small changes in revenue equal large changes in profit in both directions. Clark believes the cycle has played into Sims' favour and that investors should sell or reduce while conditions are good rather than hold through the inevitable downcycle.
quote: I look I the company's done well recently but this has been a business which has got a lot of moving parts and a lot of those moving parts are completely outside of its control I think they're very good at controlling what they can control and it's got a good management team the move into America's actually I think been a pretty good one for it but it's really cyclical and you're you always feel like you're sort of one announcement closer to something coming out of left field that that destroys the case for owning it so I'd actually be a cell because I think the cycle at the moment has played into their favor and it's been really strong and maybe that keeps going for another year or two years with Trump you can see that that could easily be the case but you know if you look historically it is a cycle and the down cycles are brutal and the up cycles are great because they've got very high fixed costs and small increments at their revenue line equal big increments at their profit line.

headline: Ben Clark holds Stockland as contrarian play despite house-and-land headwinds, flagging data center pivot
reasoning: Stockland beat guidance on pretty much every measure and had a strong pop on the day. However, the collapse of Baffler, the largest house-and-land developer in the country, has sent negative sentiment through the sector. House and land packages face severe industry headwinds with almost every moving part going against operators. That said, Stockland's balance sheet is strong at 22% debt to equity, it trades around NTA on about 12 times earnings with a near 6% dividend yield, and its data center pivot is generating actual earnings growth. Clark takes a contrarian view that bad news may already be priced in.
quote: the balance sheet of Stocklands great 22% debt to equity it looks cheap it's trading on 12 times around NTA and a near 6% dividend yield so valuation looks good I guess the contrarian in me says this is actually a time you should be looking at these sort of businesses because the news does feel like it is as bad as could be and that's typically reflected in the in the share prices and then they've got this pivot to to data centers which has driven you know we're seeing actual earnings growth coming through it's not doesn't feel like it's just narrative so I'll go ahold Andrew because I can't bring myself to say bye yet.

quote: I'd be less pessimistic than Andrew although I think some of his points are valid... and actually I'm block which I can serve a great business had a an earnings beat and an upgrade yes result zip I'd be less pessimistic than Andrew.

headline: Ben Clark holds Zip Co citing strong US consumer, 30% revenue growth and sub-2% bad debts but warns it needs close watching
reasoning: Clark is less pessimistic than Coleman, arguing that BNPL's very short credit cycle (25% of debt repaid in a fortnight) makes it much lower risk than subprime mortgages. Many BNPL users choose the product for convenience rather than necessity. The weak spot in the result was lack of merchant growth, which is important for traffic. The US consumer is in good shape which matters for Zip's North American rollout. Revenue is growing 30% per annum and bad debts are sub-2%, though declining from 40% growth earlier. Management has done a good job but the stock requires close monitoring and is not for the faint-hearted.
quote: I'd be less pessimistic than Andrew although I think some of his points are valid they are a lender but the cycle in which their lending is very short and I think there's a lot less risk than say subprime etc 30-year mortgages are different to eight-year debts where 25% of the debt is paid upfront and we've been you know two weeks you've been paid half your money back so and I do think that a lot of people yes there's a large demographic that maybe are challenged to go elsewhere but I know a lot of people who use buy now pay later who certainly can pay by other means if they wanted to it's just they like to do it that way... the poor spot of zips result was that there wasn't a lot of merchant growth and that's important to look for... the numbers are impressive they're growing 30% per annum and it was 40% per annum fairly recently bad and doubtful debts sub 2% that can turn you do need to be watching stocks like this very closely and not for the faint-hearted.

headline: Ben Clark holds 2S unconvincingly as a binary regulatory outcome with enough cash to cover any fine
reasoning: 2S has had very strong revenue and profit growth but the Simba-One merger in Singapore collapsed and regulators are investigating alleged unauthorised use of spectrum. The share price has fallen more than 70% this year and there has been no company update since May. The outcome is binary: if the penalty is mild or the company is cleared, the stock is seriously cheap and will rerate sharply; if the licence is revoked the downside is severe. On the positive side 2S has about $1 of cash per share, so at current prices only $1 of enterprise value is being ascribed to the business and a large fine could be funded without a capital raise.
quote: it if if it's fairly mild or they find found not to have done the wrong thing the stock looks seriously cheap and it's going to have a massive rerate and you know I guess the one thing I'd say is a lot of bad news has been priced in but maybe that's right so if I was in it I probably hold it but I wouldn't be buying it without knowing what I'm buying... it's got a dollar in share per a dollar per share in cash so you're now only paying a dollar of enterprise value for the business and if there is a big fine which it sounds like there could be they won't have to raise capital to fund it.

headline: Ben Clark would sell Integral Diagnostics citing persistent management churn and earnings disappointments
reasoning: Despite agreeing with the positive industry backdrop and dominant market position, Clark has been consistently disappointed by Integral Diagnostics' inability to capitalise on its position. The company has had a 'clearing of the decks' every year for two to three years with another pre-release before the August result. Both the CEO and CFO have now departed. The share price has essentially halved from COVID-era highs and has gone nowhere for three to four years because earnings have been very jumpy. At 17 times Clark sees better healthcare alternatives such as ResMed, Fisher & Paykel Healthcare, and CSL.
quote: I'd be less keen I think it's I think it's actually been a pretty poor performer it's it feels like this is a business that's had a clearing of the decks every year for the last two or three years and we saw another one in this pre-release before their August result the CEO's gone the CFO has also gone so we've got a new management team who you know put out a new vision for the business like from my point of view I agree with everything Andrew's saying in terms of the industry backdrop and their position but to me they've never really shown shareholders an ability to take advantage of that in that you know we seem to get constant excuses as to why things haven't been going as well as expected and I think the share price chart tells you that you know it's it's really well it's halved over five years that was the COVID back in 2021 but you know it's done nothing for three or four years and it's really because the earnings have been very jumpy.

headline: Ben Clark holds Centuria Capital as cheap with most pain priced in, highlighting unique data center AI compute exposure

This gives Centuria a unique and underappreciated exposure to AI infrastructure. The stock trades on a low earnings multiple with manageable gearing and a headline yield, though that yield may be cut. Clark cannot bring himself to buy but believes most of the pain is already reflected in the share price.
quote: an interesting part is reset data which is a business that I'm Centuria owns I think 50% of and so what might not be commonly known is there are three companies in Australia that have the license to to effectively buy the Blackwell Nvidia trip chips and and they're forming Neocloud businesses effectively and leasing out that computing power the other two ones called thermos which will be floating next year I think and Sharon AI is a second which will float pretty soon I think and and reset data has the third license which is pretty important because if you look at this space through CDC isn't it no it's um it's one of the three so Australia is a tier one a tier one friend of the United States has very few countries that Nvidia's are actually allowed to sell these chips too and there are three companies in Australia that have the license to rent out buy these chips and rent out the computing power which reset data is by far the smallest and it's at its earlier stage... look aside from that it looks very cheap it's trading on a very low earnings multiple gearing is not an issue it's it's it doesn't have a lot of debt so that's a big tick when things go against you in this space headline yield looks good but I'd be wary that that's probably going to get cut I'll be a whole just because I think most of the pain is now in the share price but I couldn't bring myself to buy it.

headline: Ben Clark holds Data 3 as high quality AI tailwind beneficiary but prefers to wait for a lower entry multiple

However, the share price has been more volatile than earnings, which has historically provided frequent opportunities to buy at lower multiples than today's 31x PE. He would hold a position but does not think now is the time to rush in.

Resources have absolutely been a highlight. I think that they've broadly beaten and it's been good to see I think some of the beaten up so-called quality stocks continuing to just report really good numbers and it feels like the market's starting to buy into the story that they're not going to get disrupted by AI and starting to look properly at the businesses again so that's been good for us.

headline: Ben Clark sells Star Entertainment citing unresolved regulatory overhang, unknown large fine, structural competitive disadvantage and excess debt
reasoning: Star still faces a large and unquantified regulatory fine. The casino is effectively being run by a gambling authority-appointed administrator because Star is not deemed ready to manage it independently. The property situation remains a major issue and the balance sheet carries too much debt. Structurally Star is at a competitive disadvantage: poker machines in NSW pubs require no identity declaration, while Star's regulatory framework requires full disclosure, effectively driving away the cash-based customers who previously underpinned volumes.
quote: this company there's still a lot of regulatory stuff they've still got this massive there were so many things that there's a there's a big fine coming their way and they don't know what it how much it's going to be they they I believe the casino is still being run effectively by someone who the gambling authorities have put into run it because they don't see that they're ready to run it themselves again there's the property issue which is a big issue and then there's still way too much debt on the balance sheet and you know I think from a structural point of view the biggest issue this company's got is that you can go into any pub around New South Wales and put as much money as you want into poker machines and not have to tell anyone who you are but if you do that at the star because of the regulatory framework that they're under it all is has to be declared etc etc so we know a lot of the money that goes through this machines is not the cleanest sort of money in the world so they're kind of fighting a fight with one arm time behind their back and I can't see any reason you want to be in star.
